definition:
Regeneration, or the new birth, is God's act of giving spiritual life to people who cannot give it to themselves. Scripture describes human beings apart from grace not merely as weak or misinformed but as having hearts turned away from God, and it describes salvation as including a new beginning at the root: a new heart, a new spirit, a birth “of God” (John 1:13), a resurrection from the dead, a new creation. Regeneration is the inward side of salvation, what God does in a person, as justification is what God declares about a person. It is the work of the Holy Spirit, usually through the word of the gospel, and it shows itself in faith in Christ, repentance, love, and a changed life. The Bible also speaks of a regeneration of the whole world at the end, and the new birth of individuals is its first installment.

The Hebrew Bible has no single technical word for it. It speaks instead in pictures: God giving a lev chadash, ‘a new heart’, and a ruach chadashah, ‘a new spirit’ (Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26); God circumcising the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6); and God creating a clean heart, with the verb bara', ‘create’, which in its basic form the Old Testament uses only with God as subject (Psalm 51:10). The Greek New Testament has several terms. Palingenesia, ‘regeneration’ or ‘renewal’, appears only twice, once of the renewal of all things (Matthew 19:28) and once of personal salvation, “the washing of new birth” (Titus 3:5). Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born anōthen, an adverb that can mean ‘again’ or ‘from above’ (John 3:3, 7); Nicodemus hears the first, John elsewhere uses the word for the second (John 3:31), and many interpreters think the double sense is intended. Peter uses anagennaō, ‘to cause to be born again’ (1 Peter 1:3, 23); James uses apokueō, ‘to give birth’ (James 1:18); and John's first letter repeatedly speaks of those ‘born of God’. Related expressions include ‘new creation’ (kainē ktisis) and ‘made alive together with’ (syzōopoieō).
ot:
The Old Testament lays the ground by diagnosing a problem at the level of the heart, which in Hebrew is the center of thought, will, and desire, not only of feeling. Before the flood “every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time” (Genesis 6:5), and after it God says the same of humanity that survives, “every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21). The flood cleansed the earth but not the heart. Israel's own history confirms the diagnosis. At the end of the wilderness years Moses tells the people, “to this day the LORD has not given you a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear” (Deuteronomy 29:4). Jeremiah asks, “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Neither are you able to do good” (Jeremiah 13:23), and he says, “The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure” (Jeremiah 17:9).

The law and the prophets speak to this condition in two ways that stand side by side. They command: “Circumcise your hearts” (Deuteronomy 10:16); “remove the foreskins of your hearts” (Jeremiah 4:4); “fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you die, O house of Israel?” (Ezekiel 18:31). And they promise that God himself will do what they command. Circumcision was the sign of belonging to the covenant people; to circumcise the heart meant to remove what shut the person off from God. Deuteronomy looks past the exile it foresees to a day when “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live” (Deuteronomy 30:6). The command shows what God rightly requires; the promise shows that he intends to supply it. Christian traditions relate the two differently, but all of them read the pair together.

The promise grows clearer in the prophets of the exile, the years after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Jeremiah hears God say, “I will give them a heart to know Me” (Jeremiah 24:7), and promises a new covenant in which God will “put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), a covenant in which “they will all know Me” (Jeremiah 31:34). Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles in Babylon, gives the fullest form: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:26-27). The promise begins with cleansing water, “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25), and it is joined to God's concern for his own name (Ezekiel 36:22). In the next chapter the prophet sees a valley of dry bones and is asked, “Son of man, can these bones come to life?” (Ezekiel 37:3). The same Hebrew word, ruach, means ‘breath’, ‘wind’, and ‘spirit’, and the vision plays on all three: God breathes into the slain, and the promise is interpreted, “I will put My Spirit in you and you will live” (Ezekiel 37:14). Isaiah adds the image of water on dry ground and the Spirit poured on Israel's offspring, who will each say, “I belong to the LORD” (Isaiah 44:3-5).

Two cautions keep the reading honest. First, in their setting these promises are addressed to Israel as a people, promising national restoration after exile; the New Testament applies them to individuals in Christ and to the renewed people of God, Jew and Gentile, without dropping the corporate hope. Second, the Old Testament also knows individuals whose hearts God has touched. David, after his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah, prays, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). He asks not for improvement but for a creation. And Isaiah's vision of “new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17) sets the renewal of hearts inside the larger renewal of the world.
nt:
John's Gospel introduces the new birth in its prologue. To those who received the Word, “to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God”, “children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God” (John 1:12-13). Human descent, human desire, and human decision are all set aside as the source; the birth is from God. Then comes the conversation with Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the Jewish ruling council, who comes to Jesus by night. Jesus tells him, “no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again” (John 3:3), and when Nicodemus asks how a grown man can be born a second time, Jesus answers, “no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit” (John 3:5). The phrase has been read of Christian baptism (the view of the Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran churches and many others), of natural birth followed by spiritual birth, and of the cleansing water and Spirit promised in Ezekiel 36:25-27; Calvin, in his commentary on John, took water and Spirit as one thing, the Spirit who cleanses like water. Jesus' rebuke, “You are Israel's teacher” and yet “you do not understand these things?” (John 3:10), suggests that Nicodemus should have known the promise from the prophets. Jesus adds an image built on the double meaning of the Greek pneuma, ‘wind’ and ‘spirit’: “The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit” (John 3:8). The new birth is real and visible in its effects, but its working belongs to God. The same Gospel says, “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:63), and “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him” (John 6:44).

The apostles describe the same reality with other images. Acts tells of Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth at Philippi: “The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul's message” (Acts 16:14). Paul speaks of new creation, echoing the first words of Genesis: the God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” has “made His light shine in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4:6), and “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17; compare Galatians 6:15). He speaks of resurrection: “you were dead in your trespasses and sins”, but God, “rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses” (Ephesians 2:1, 4-5; compare Colossians 2:13). Then, “it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God”, and believers are “God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (Ephesians 2:8-10). In Titus, God “saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5), a verse that ties the new birth to the Spirit and, most interpreters agree, alludes to baptism, though traditions differ on how the washing and the new birth are related. Paul also calls believers to “put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24; compare Colossians 3:10), showing that the new beginning is meant to be lived out.

James and Peter tie the new birth to the word. “He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation” (James 1:18); “you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God” (1 Peter 1:23), and Peter adds that this word is the gospel “that was proclaimed to you” (1 Peter 1:25). God “has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). The new birth is joined to Jesus' resurrection: his rising is the source of the believer's new life.

John's first letter gives the marks of those born of God. “Everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him” (1 John 2:29); “Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God” (1 John 4:7); “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God” (1 John 5:1); and “everyone born of God overcomes the world” (1 John 5:4). The verb ‘has been born’ is a Greek perfect, describing a past event with lasting results, and Reformed interpreters often read these verses as showing that the new birth comes before and produces faith, love, and righteousness; others reply that John is giving evidence of the new birth, not setting out a sequence, and that a perfect tense alone cannot settle the order. John also writes that “Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin” (1 John 3:9), which must be read beside his warning that “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8): the one born of God does not make a settled way of life out of sin, though he still sins and confesses. Finally, the new birth of persons belongs to the renewal of everything. Jesus speaks of “the renewal of all things” (Matthew 19:28), using palingenesia, and Paul says creation itself waits to be “brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God” (Romans 8:21).

keyTexts.why: God promises to circumcise the hearts of his people so that they will love him. What the law commanded in Deuteronomy 10:16, God undertakes to do.
David asks God to create a clean heart in him, using the verb reserved for God's own creating. Repentance reaches for a new creation, not a repair.
The new covenant promises the law written on the heart and a people who all know the LORD. The New Testament hears this fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 8:8-12).
Clean water, a new heart, a new spirit, and God's own Spirit within. The fullest Old Testament promise of the new birth and the likely background of Jesus' words about water and Spirit.
Dry bones live when God's breath enters them. The vision pictures new life as resurrection, God's act on the helpless.
Those who receive Christ become children born not of human will but of God. The source of the new birth is stated in the Gospel's first chapter.
Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born again, of water and the Spirit. The classic text, with its images of birth from above and the free wind of the Spirit.
Anyone in Christ is a new creation. The new birth is placed within God's new creation begun in the risen Jesus.
The dead in sin are made alive with Christ by grace. The passage joins new life, grace, faith, and good works in one sequence.
God saved us through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, not by our righteous deeds. The only personal use of palingenesia in the New Testament.
God chose to give us birth through the word of truth. The new birth is God's decision and comes through his word.
Believers are born again of imperishable seed through the living word of God, which is the gospel preached to them. The new birth produces sincere love.
Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God and overcomes the world. The marks of the new birth are faith, love, and obedience.

history:
The early church connected the new birth closely with baptism, reading John 3:5 and Titus 3:5 together. Justin Martyr, describing Christian worship to the Roman emperor in his First Apology (about AD 155, chapter 61), explains that those who believe and resolve to live accordingly are brought to water and are ‘regenerated’ in the way Christians themselves were, and he cites Jesus' words about being born again. The same link runs through the fathers of East and West. Augustine of Hippo, in his controversy with Pelagius in the early fifth century, insisted that fallen human beings need not only forgiveness but the healing of the will by grace, which must come first if anyone is to believe and love God. Pelagius's teaching was condemned at the Council of Carthage (418) and the Council of Ephesus (431), and the Council of Orange (529) taught that even the beginning of faith and the desire to believe are gifts of grace, not the natural achievement of the will. Medieval theology, summed up in Thomas Aquinas, taught that baptism removes the guilt of original sin and infuses grace and the virtues, and the Council of Trent reaffirmed this in its decrees of 1546 and 1547, condemning the reading of John 3:5 as a mere metaphor for the Spirit (Session VII, canons on baptism, canon 2).

The Reformers kept the new birth at the center of salvation but divided over its relation to the sacraments. Martin Luther's Small Catechism (1529) calls baptism, on the basis of Titus 3:5, a washing of regeneration, effective not by water alone but by the word of God with the water and received by faith. John Calvin used ‘regeneration’ broadly for the whole lifelong renewal of the believer, identifying it with repentance (Institutes 3.3.9). The Anabaptists' Schleitheim Confession (1527) restricted baptism to those who had learned repentance and amendment of life, making the new birth the condition of baptism rather than its effect. In the Netherlands, the Remonstrants' five articles (1610) affirmed that a person must be born again of God in Christ by the Holy Spirit in order to think or do anything truly good, but held that this grace can be resisted. The Synod of Dort answered in its Canons (1619, Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine, articles 11 and 12) that regeneration is a supernatural work of God, not merely moral persuasion, likened to creation and to raising the dead, by which the will is made alive and then itself believes. Later Reformed theology generally narrowed ‘regeneration’ to this first imparting of life and distinguished it from conversion and sanctification.

The evangelical revivals of the eighteenth century made the new birth their banner. George Whitefield's sermon The Nature and Necessity of Our New Birth in Christ Jesus, preached in Bristol and published in 1737, became his signature message. Jonathan Edwards, in A Divine and Supernatural Light (1734) and A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections (1746), described the new birth as God giving a new spiritual sense of the beauty of divine things, and warned against judging it by the intensity of emotion. John Wesley's sermon The New Birth (1760) called justification and the new birth the two fundamental doctrines of Christianity, the first what God does for us in forgiving, the second what God does in us in renewing our fallen nature. The question of baptism returned in the Church of England when the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council ruled in March 1850, in the Gorham case, that a clergyman who denied that baptism always regenerates infants could hold office; Charles Spurgeon's sermon Baptismal Regeneration (5 June 1864) attacked the Prayer Book's teaching from a Baptist position. In America, Charles Finney's Sermons on Important Subjects (1836) included Sinners Bound to Change Their Own Hearts, which treated the change of heart as the sinner's own moral choice, a view his Reformed contemporaries strongly opposed. In the twentieth century ‘born again’ became a public label, especially in the United States in 1976, when Jimmy Carter's description of himself as born again drew national attention and Newsweek named it the year of the evangelical, and Charles Colson's memoir Born Again appeared the same year. The site's page on how we are saved surveys the debate over grace and the will that surrounds this doctrine.

differ.body: Reformed theology teaches that those dead in sin cannot believe until God makes them alive, so the new birth comes first in logical order, though not necessarily in time, and faith and repentance are its first fruits. It is monergistic, the work of God alone, and effectual: the Spirit, usually through the preached word, so renews the will that the person freely and gladly comes to Christ. Defenders point to John 1:13, which excludes the will of man as the source; to Ephesians 2:5, where God makes the dead alive; to Acts 16:14, where the Lord opens Lydia's heart; to the perfect tense of 1 John 5:1; and to the Canons of Dort (1619). They hold that this is the only account in which no one can boast of having supplied the decisive difference.

differ.view: Prevenient grace, then faith and new birth (Wesleyan and Arminian)
differ.body: Arminian and Wesleyan theologians agree that fallen people cannot turn to God by their own power. They teach that God's prevenient grace, the grace that goes before, is given widely, restoring enough freedom that a person can respond to the gospel or refuse it. When a person believes, God justifies and regenerates them together, so that the new birth follows or accompanies faith rather than causing it. Defenders note that John 1:12 speaks of those who received Christ being given the right to become children of God, that Scripture everywhere calls hearers to believe and warns against resisting the Spirit (Acts 7:51), and that the Remonstrance (1610) and Wesley both taught the necessity of the new birth while holding that grace can be resisted.

differ.view: Baptismal regeneration (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and many Anglicans)
differ.body: These churches teach that God gives the new birth through baptism, joining water to his word and Spirit as Jesus says in John 3:5 and Paul in Titus 3:5, and as 1 Peter 3:21 says baptism now saves. The gift is God's act, not the minister's or the recipient's work, and it is given to infants as well as adults. Lutherans stress that baptism works by the word and is received by faith, which God can create in an infant, and that the grace given can be rejected and lost and is returned to daily in repentance. Catholic teaching holds that baptism frees from sin and brings rebirth as children of God (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1213). The Orthodox join baptism with chrismation as the beginning of life in Christ. All hold that the new birth must be lived in faith and repentance.

differ.view: New birth by Spirit and word, with baptism as its sign (Baptist and believers' church)
differ.body: Baptists and other believers' churches, both Calvinist and non-Calvinist, teach that the Spirit gives new birth through the word of the gospel (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23) when a person believes, and that baptism is the public sign and confession of a new birth that has already happened. They read Titus 3:5 and John 3:5 as speaking of the Spirit's cleansing, pictured in baptism but not given by it, and point to the thief on the cross and to Cornelius's household, who received the Spirit before being baptized (Acts 10:44-48). They argue that tying the new birth to the rite risks assuring the unconverted, the concern Spurgeon pressed in 1864, and they reserve baptism for those who profess faith.

errors:
The first error the church rejected is that people do not need a new birth at all, only better teaching, a good example, or greater effort. Pelagius held that human nature was not so damaged by Adam's sin that it could not obey God, and the councils of Carthage (418), Ephesus (431), and Orange (529) rejected his teaching. Jesus' words to Nicodemus, a devout teacher of the law, show that religious seriousness is not the same as new life. A modern form of the same error treats the new birth as a moral fresh start the person makes for himself, a resolution rather than a gift. Every major tradition, whatever its view of the will, confesses that the new birth is God's work by his Spirit.

Other distortions are narrower. One treats baptism or any rite as automatically producing life apart from faith, so that a person can rest in having been baptized while living in open unbelief; the traditions that teach baptismal regeneration reject this, insisting that the gift must be received in faith and lived in repentance. Another equates the new birth with a particular emotional experience or a datable decision, so that believers who cannot name a moment are told they are not born again, or people who made a decision are assured regardless of how they live. Scripture's tests are faith in Jesus, love, and righteousness (1 John 2:29; 4:7; 5:1), not a single kind of experience, and Jesus' image of the wind warns against making the Spirit's working follow a pattern. A third misreads 1 John 3:9 as teaching that the born again no longer sin at all, a claim the same letter rejects (1 John 1:8-9).
life:
The doctrine of the new birth is humbling and hopeful at once. It is humbling because it says that no one is too good to need it; Nicodemus was a respected teacher and still had to be born again. It is hopeful because it says no one is too far gone to receive it. God's question to Ezekiel over the valley of bones, whether they can live, is the question every parent, friend, or pastor asks over someone who seems beyond reach, and the answer in that vision was not the bones' strength but God's breath. The doctrine frees people to pray for others with confidence and to speak the gospel plainly, since God gives life through his word.

It also brings patience and honesty to how a Christian reads his own life. The wind blows where it wishes, and people come to faith in many ways, some suddenly and some so gradually they cannot name the day. What matters is not the story of the beginning but the signs of life now: trust in Christ, love for other believers, a desire to do what is right, and a readiness to confess sin. Those signs are often weak. A newborn is still newly born. The new birth is the start of a life that will grow, and it is the first taste of the renewal God has promised for the whole creation.
questions: Deuteronomy 10:16 commands Israel to circumcise their hearts, and Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that God will do it. How do the command and the promise fit together, and where does Ezekiel 18:31 and 36:26 show the same pattern?
Jesus tells Nicodemus that the Spirit is like the wind (John 3:8). What does this image say about how the new birth happens, and how might it correct the way people describe conversion?
1 John names faith, love, and righteousness as marks of those born of God. How can these marks give assurance without turning into a checklist that either flatters or crushes?
